title: ReAct Breakdown: How ICLR 2023 Defines the Agent Paradigm with a Loop
subtitle: Reading a Foundational Work from the Perspective of Structural Anatomy
markdown: > Breakdown Target: ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models, ICLR 2023 (notable top-5%). Authors are from Princeton University and Google Research Brain, with first author Shunyu Yao, who is also a core author of Tree of Thoughts, SWE-bench, and SWE-agent. This article does only one thing: analyze why the structure of this paper is good. All numbers come from the latest arXiv version of the paper's main text, which can be cross-checked with the original tables. ## 1. Why It Is Worth Breaking Down The skeleton of almost all subsequent work in the agent direction grows on ReAct: a single loop where thought, action, and observation are interleaved. From tool calling in the ChatGPT plugin era, to reasoning-then-searching in Search-R1, to the executors in today's various agent frameworks, the underlying layer is all ReAct. The baseline agent evaluated by WebRL on WebArena is ReAct, and the Actor in Reflexion directly reuses it. A minimalist design of 'interleaved generation' supports an entire research direction. Such papers are naturally structural templates: the method section has only one part, and all persuasiveness comes from the organization of the experiments. ## 2. The Skeleton of the Six Main Sections | Section | Responsibility | Breakdown Key Points | | --- | --- | --- | | 1 Introduction | Establishing the Argument | Figure 1's four-panel comparison tells the essence of the method in one image | | 2 ReAct | Method | No subsections, occupies only two pages, including a list of four major characteristics | | 3 Knowledge-Intensive Reasoning Tasks | First Half of Experiments | HotpotQA / FEVER, with built-in setup / methods / results | | 4 Decision Making Tasks | Second Half of Experiments | ALFWorld / WebShop, symmetric structure to the first half | | 5 Related Work | Positioning | Move to Section 5; after a dual-thread review, highlight the differences with SayCan and Inner Monologue | | 6 Conclusion | Wrap-up | Half a page | Two structural decisions are worth noting. First, placing the related work section later: when the method is intuitive enough, letting readers understand it first before exploring the genealogy minimizes reading friction. Second, the experiments are split symmetrically by task type, separately answering whether reasoning helps action on reasoning tasks and whether reasoning helps action on decision-making tasks; only together do these two halves support the term "Synergizing" in the title. ## III. Establishing the Argument with One Figure: The Four-Panel Comparison in Figure 1 The Introduction runs four prompts on the same HotpotQA question: Standard answers directly, CoT reasons only, Act acts only, and ReAct interleaves. Before encountering any formulas, readers visually perceive where the differences arise: Act-only blindly searches, CoT follows erroneous memories and fabricates, while ReAct processes observations before each action step. The Method section logically needs to do only one thing: expand the action space to A ∪ L, where thoughts in the language space L serve six purposes (decomposing goals, injecting commonsense, extracting key information, tracking progress, handling anomalies, synthesizing answers). The simpler the method, the more effort must be invested in writing to ensure readers understand it at first glance; Figure 1 fulfills this function. ## IV. Failure Mode Analysis: Table 2 is an Underrated Treasure Based on 200 manually annotated samples, the success and failure patterns of ReAct and CoT are presented in the same table: | Pattern | ReAct | CoT | | --- | --- | --- | | Hallucination in successful cases (false positives) | 6% | 14% | | Proportion of failures caused by hallucination | 0% | 56% | | Reasoning errors in failure cases | 47% | 16% | | Search results provide no information (unique to ReAct) | 23% | Not applicable | This table honestly reports its own weaknesses: ReAct's structural constraints lead to a higher rate of reasoning errors and repeated generation of previous actions. However, this honest analysis directly led to the paper's best result: since ReAct excels in factuality and CoT excels in flexibility, the combination was adopted. The mixed prompt of ReAct and CoT-SC achieved 35.1 EM on HotpotQA and 64.6 on FEVER, outperforming either method used alone. A well-executed failure analysis naturally generates the next step's plan; this is the compound interest of experimental design. ## 5. Organization of Two Key Sets of Numbers On knowledge-intensive tasks, ReAct actually slightly underperforms CoT on HotpotQA (27.4 EM vs. 29.4). The paper does not shy away from this but instead shifts the narrative focus to the respective strengths of reasoning and action. On decision-making tasks, however, it achieves overwhelming victory: 71% on ALFWorld compared to the imitation learning baseline BUTLER's 37%, and a success rate of 40.0% on WebShop compared to IL+RL's 28.7%. ReAct used only 1 to 2 in-context examples, while its opponents used 10³ to 10⁵ training trajectories. The final piece of the puzzle is the fine-tuning loop: fine-tuning with only 3,000 correct trajectories generated by ReAct allowed PaLM-8B to surpass all PaLM-62B prompting methods, and 62B surpassed all 540B prompting methods. The clue planted in Section 3.2 regarding the combination of internal and external knowledge converges in the scaling curve of Figure 3, creating a coherent narrative from start to finish. ## 6. Three Writing Techniques Worth Adopting 1. **Establish the argument with one figure**: Figure 1 compares four prompting methods using the same question, completing the argument for the method's differentiated claim in the Introduction; everything that follows serves as evidence. 2. **Symmetrical experiments across two task families**: Knowledge-intensive and decision-making tasks each occupy a section, with symmetrical structure that jointly supports the claim of 'generality.' Single-sided experiments cannot support the claim of 'Synergizing.' 3. **All prompts are relegated to Appendix C**: The main text remains clean, and the four complete prompt templates are copied verbatim for reproducibility; the reproducibility commitment is fulfilled by the appendix. ## Footnotes: Mapping to My Own Work The six uses of 'thought' in ReAct are almost the prompt skeleton for the post-match coaching system's 'behavioral diagnosis → temporal attribution' phase: extracting key information from observations, tracking task progress, and adjusting plans when anomalies occur. The hallucination rate comparison in Table 2 (6% vs. 14%) corroborates the conclusion of OKC-SFT from another angle: when the reasoning process has external evidence to rely on, the hallucination rate can be systematically reduced (we reduced it from 34.4% to 15.6%). The algorithm layer outputs structured evidence, and every step of thought in the LLM layer is traceable; this is the same thing as ReAct ensuring that every answer is preceded by an observation. ## References - Paper: arXiv:2210.03629, published at ICLR 2023 (notable top-5%) - Code and prompt templates: github.com/ysymyth/ReAct - Main experimental scope: HotpotQA and FEVER as knowledge-intensive tasks (PaLM-540B prompting), ALFWorld and WebShop as decision-making tasks (best of 6 and single-shot evaluation)
